title: jQuery selectors and DOM manipulation: legacy library literacy
learningObjectives: Explain jquery selectors and dom manipulation: legacy library literacy and the problem it addresses.
Use the relevant language or browser API with valid syntax.
Compare the technique with modern alternatives and identify when each is appropriate.
Handle errors, boundaries, security, and compatibility deliberately.
Test the implementation and explain its behaviour with evidence.

understand.concept: jQuery is a JavaScript library that historically simplified DOM selection, event handling, animation, and AJAX across older browser environments. Its $ function returns a jQuery collection, and methods such as .text(), .addClass(), .on(), and .find() operate on that collection. Modern browser APIs provide native alternatives such as querySelector, classList, addEventListener, fetch, and textContent. When maintaining a jQuery project, understand whether the collection contains zero, one, or many elements, avoid unsafe .html() insertion with untrusted data, and verify the library version and plugin dependencies. Do not add jQuery to a new project without a clear requirement.
understand.whyItMatters: Legacy websites and plugins may still depend on jQuery. Developers should be able to read, debug, and gradually modernize that code without assuming the library is required for current browser work.
understand.analogy: jQuery is a convenience toolkit that wraps common browser operations in a consistent collection-based API.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy can make jQuery sound like a browser requirement; it is an optional library, not part of the JavaScript language.

explain.narrative: Compare a jQuery selector and text update with the equivalent native DOM code. Explain how a jQuery collection differs from a single DOM element.

examples.explanation: The jQuery selector returns a collection and the methods update text and add a class. This assumes jQuery has already been loaded and available as $.
examples.expectedOutput: The element with id status displays Ready and receives the is-ready class.

examples.explanation: The native DOM version uses querySelector, textContent, and classList without a library dependency.
examples.expectedOutput: The same visible result is produced using browser APIs.

practise.guidedTask: Read a small jQuery module and annotate each selector, collection operation, event handler, and DOM update. Reproduce the behaviour with native browser APIs.
practise.independentTask: Plan a gradual migration from jQuery to native APIs. Preserve event delegation, plugin behaviour, and test coverage; remove the dependency only when no remaining code requires it.
hints: A jQuery collection is not the same thing as a single DOM element.
Prefer .text() or native textContent for untrusted text, not .html().
Check plugin and version dependencies before removing the library.

questions.prompt: Is jQuery part of the JavaScript language specification?
options: No, it is an optional JavaScript library
Yes, it is a built-in browser object
questions.answer: No, it is an optional JavaScript library
questions.explanation: jQuery is a library distributed separately from the JavaScript language.
The selector returns a jQuery collection of matched elements.

questions.prompt: Which jQuery method sets text content safely?
questions.explanation: text() sets text content without interpreting it as HTML.

questions.prompt: Which native API adds an event listener?
questions.explanation: addEventListener registers a handler for an event on an EventTarget.

questions.prompt: When should a new project add jQuery?
options: Only when a clear dependency or compatibility requirement justifies it
questions.answer: Only when a clear dependency or compatibility requirement justifies it
questions.explanation: Modern browsers provide native APIs; add a library only when its benefits justify the dependency.
